title: The spare keys
bodyMd:
Original literary narrative.

When my aunt asked me to take over the harbor office for a week, she handed me a ring of keys heavy enough to pull my coat sideways. Each bore a neat paper label. The smallest key had no label at all. "You probably won't need that one," she said.

On Monday I used the labeled keys confidently. They opened the filing cabinet, the equipment cupboard, and the drawer of visitor permits. By Tuesday I had decided that managing the office meant knowing where everything belonged. I corrected the crooked labels on the shelves. I even arranged the pencils by length.

Then Mr. Vale arrived carrying an empty glass jar. He did not want a permit. He wanted to sit by the office window until his daughter's boat returned. I began to explain that the waiting room was locked, and that the key was not among the labeled ones. He pointed at the smallest key. "Your aunt never bothered to name that room," he said. "Everyone knows what it's for."

The door opened onto three worn chairs and a kettle. From the window we could see the channel. Mr. Vale set the jar on the sill; it was for the shells his daughter always brought him. I left my pencils in their uneven row and filled the kettle. For the first time that week, the office seemed properly in order.
